The C compiler is written in C. To build a new one, you use the previous one. That chain of “the old compiler builds the new one” is the point Thompson is going to exploit.
He modifies the compiler so that, when it detects it is compiling the login program, it secretly adds a master password. The login code looks clean; the binary already carries the backdoor.
He teaches the compiler to recognize when it is compiling ITSELF and to insert both tricks again into the new compiler. It's a program that replicates inside its own build tool.

Now he removes both tricks from the compiler's source code. They're no longer needed: the binary carries them and passes them on to every generation. Anyone reviewing the source code finds nothing unusual.

“You can't trust code that you did not totally create yourself.” Reviewing the source code isn't enough: you have to trust (or verify) the whole chain — compilers, tools and the people who made them. Today it's countered with reproducible builds and by compiling from several independent sources.
Born on February 4, 1943 in New Orleans. He studied electrical engineering at the University of California, Berkeley (bachelor's 1965, master's 1966) and joined Bell Labs in 1966.
Together with Dennis Ritchie, he created Unix on a PDP-7 computer left unused after Bell Labs withdrew from the Multics project. Linux, macOS, Android and a good part of the Internet descend from it.
He wrote B, the direct ancestor of C (the language Ritchie developed from it).
He brought regular expressions to text editors (ed) and created grep in 1973 to search for patterns in files: every security professional uses it today.
With Joe Condon he built Belle, the world computer chess champion in 1980. Its endgame databases revolutionized computer chess.
Co-author of Bell Labs' Plan 9. In 1992, with Rob Pike, he designed UTF-8 — the encoding that lets you write in any language and that almost the entire web uses today.
At Google, with Robert Griesemer and Rob Pike, he designed the Go language, publicly presented in 2009.
Turing Award 1983 (with Ritchie) · U.S. National Medal of Technology, 1998.
In 2019, Thompson's Unix password from the 1970s, stored in the BSD source code, was cracked: it was “p/q2-q4!”, a chess move. Even his password was a pawn move.
He is credited with the phrase: “When in doubt, use brute force”.
His C language remains the foundation of operating systems, browsers and most security software.
She created one of the first compilers and championed programming in something close to human language. She popularized the term “bug” after finding a moth in a Harvard computer in 1947.
In 1983 he started the free software movement: being able to read, modify and share code is a condition for being able to trust it.
In 1991 he published the Linux kernel, now present in most of the world's servers and in Android.
In 1991 he published PGP so anyone could encrypt their email: privacy as a right.
Famous for social engineering: he showed that tricking a person is often easier than breaking a machine.

The adult human skeleton has 206 bones, although we are born with about 300 — many fuse as we grow.
The human heart beats on average 100,000 times a day, pumping blood through about 100,000 km of blood vessels.
Human lungs have about 300 million tiny air sacs (alveoli) where oxygen exchange takes place.
The human small intestine is about 6-7 meters long — coiled inside the abdomen to fit in so little space.
The human brain has about 86 billion neurons, communicating with each other at speeds of up to 120 meters per second.
The bull's skeleton is adapted to support a lot of body weight, with especially robust leg bones.
The heart of an adult bull can weigh more than 2 kg — several times the size of a human heart.
Bulls have large lungs that allow them sustained physical effort for grazing and moving long distances.
The bull's stomach has 4 chambers (rumen, reticulum, omasum, abomasum) because it is a ruminant — that's how it digests grass and cellulose that humans can't use.
Bulls have panoramic vision of almost 330° thanks to the lateral position of their eyes, although with little frontal depth perception.
A cat has around 230 bones (more than a human) and a floating collarbone that lets it squeeze through very narrow spaces.
A cat's heart beats much faster than a human's: between 140 and 220 times per minute at rest.
Cats breathe 20 to 30 times per minute at rest, faster than an adult human.
Cats are strict carnivores — their digestive system is adapted almost exclusively to process animal protein.
A cat's whiskers are sensory organs connected to deep nerve endings, which help it detect spaces and vibrations in the dark.
Owls have twice as many neck vertebrae as humans (14 versus 7), which lets them turn their head up to 270°.
Owls have special arteries in the neck that prevent cutting off blood flow to the brain even when turning the head to the extreme.
Birds, including owls, have air sacs in addition to lungs — a more efficient respiratory system than that of mammals.
Owls swallow their prey almost whole and then regurgitate a "pellet" with the bones and fur they couldn't digest.
Owls have such precise hearing that they can hunt in total darkness guided only by sound.
